originalHypothesis.chosenHook: What if Earth had twice as much air?
originalHypothesis.firstTwoSeconds: Earth's blue atmospheric halo grows and a clear gauge jumps from 1 atm to 2 atm; brief readable TWO TIMES AIR caption
originalHypothesis.finalScene: Side-by-side at same temperature: 1 atm versus 2 atm, oxygen remains 21% by fraction while molecule count per equal volume doubles; the pressure gauge stays visibly higher. No generic CTA.
fourBeats: Air column doubles; gauge rises while Earth remains recognizable
Molecule model shows same proportions of nitrogen/oxygen but more molecules in same volume
Aircraft wing demonstrates increased drag and an approaching meteoroid meets more air without promising a specific burn-up
Final side-by-side closes the central question: same air mixture, more pressure and higher oxygen partial pressure
originalHypothesis.proposedNarration: What if Earth had twice as much air? At sea level, the air's weight would push about twice as hard. Oxygen would still make up roughly twenty-one percent. But in the same volume, there'd be more oxygen molecules. Airplanes would meet more drag. Meteors would meet more resistance. And that is the surprise: not a new oxygen mix, but more of the same gases pressing down on everything.
